newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes higher in US, assets surge on Jobs fall.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes higher in US, assets surge on Jobs fall.

text.p: The dollar was jostled by surprisingly weak U.S. employment data on Friday, but closed higher after U.S. stocks and bonds rejoiced in the belief the Federal Reserve will be reluctant to increase interest rates.
Currency traders were divided by the report. The dollar held to fairly tight ranges, but fell initially on data showing a 0.5 percent jump in monthly wages.

"The market is more sensitized to inflation than it is to growth right now," said John Nelson, senior vice president at ABN-AMRO Bank. "As a result the wage number was probably more important than the non-farm payroll number."
"But if you look at U.S. stocks and U.S. bonds...I think that will add a biddish tone to the dollar."
The dollar subsequently rose to 1.5318/23 marks from 1.5305/10 at the open and to 111.77/82 yen from 111.55/60.

Yields on U.S. Treasury yields fell and the bonds gained more than a point after the government reported U.S. payrolls contracted 40,000 last month. August non-farm payrolls were revised down to a rise of 241,000 from 250,000.
Economists polled by Reuters expected payrolls to rise 166,000 in September.

The unemployment rate also rose to 5.2 percent -- as expected -- in September, from 5.1 percent in August, diminishing the odds the Federal Reserve policy makers will chose to tighten credit when they next meet on November 13.
The Dow Jones industrial stock average surged 60 points to a new record high on Friday.

With interest rates across Europe falling and yields in Japan at record-low levels, foreigners may increasingly ignore U.S. economic data. Their appetite for dollar-denominated assets should continue to fuel the dollar's trend even if U.S. interest rates fall, as bond yields did today, traders said.
"Lower interest rates are a product of assets improving in value, not a lack of economic activity," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale.
"It's more of a product of supply and demand for U.S. assets."

Even the Fed's surprise decision to not raise short-term interest rates at its last meeting on September 24 failed to derail the dollar, which hit a two-and-a-half-year high against the yen and a three-month high versus the mark this week.
The jobs data seems to validate the Fed's decision and opens up the possibility that interest rates will remain stable in the near term, or even fall if the economy shows further signs of slowing.
"No matter what the numbers were it doesn't really change the market sentiment," said Dorit Ronnen, foreign exchange trader at Bank Leumi Trust Co.

"Typically, when you see a number like that they say: 'Okay the Fed is going to ease' and the dollar would come off, but it didn't. The bond and stock markets are well bid and the dollar followed that," she added.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2576/81 Swiss francs from 1.2570/80 at the open. It fell to Canadian $1.3543/48 from C$1.3570/75.
The pound rose to $1.5648/58 from $1.5625/32 and the Australian dollar slipped to $0.7886/91 from $0.7890/95.
